title: I highly recommend Freelancers: A Crossroads Game (review)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9h2v-rVmwEA

Daniel (@dungeondive) gives Freelancers: A Crossroads Game from Plaid Hat a strong recommendation after one solo adventure. He credits the illustrators and the writer by name, because art and prose carry it. The setup: humanity is dead and has left behind a broken gig economy, so your mutated band of freelancers will take any job. He calls it gonzo Gamma World science fantasy, both goofy and genuinely dark. A "foul-mouthed" title he picked up early triggered a later scene he never expected a board game to go near.

The structure hangs off seven table roles. The Game Master runs the browser app, which works as a huge deck of story encounters. The Bookkeeper handles the location book, where heroes are assigned to actions against a 45-second timer. The Cartographer charts paths across five very different maps, including a hexcrawl and an isometric one. Then come the Influencer, the Medic with a shared seven-wound pool, the Scout and the Lookout. The Scout's risk dial raises every target number and feeds a push-your-luck bag of time, supply and companion chips, including Lazybones the chilled DJ, eventually fed to a dragon. Characters mix a species with an absurd class such as divorcee, clam digger or dung farmer.

His only complaints are loose standee bases and too few equipment slots, which leave treasure discarded. Solo works, but the influence track and the role-play votes need a table. He closes on his app argument: don't leave good scotch undrunk because one day it'll be gone.

----

Freelancers makes you perform a rallying speech and lets the table vote on it. Do role-play prompts in board games work for your group, or do they fall flat?
